analogy.p: Think of the atmosphere as a bank account holding carbon dioxide. Photosynthesis is a **deposit** (CO2 leaves the account and is stored in plant bodies), respiration, decay and combustion are **withdrawals** put back into the account, and fossil fuels are a long-term savings account locked away for millions of years. If deposits and withdrawals are equal the balance stays steady; burning fossil fuels is like emptying the savings account into the main account very quickly, so the balance rises. The analogy breaks down because carbon atoms are not 'spent' or lost: the same atoms keep moving round, and the total amount of carbon stays the same.
analogy.t: The carbon cycle as a bank with deposits and withdrawals

bullets: **Materials are recycled** in ecosystems so that the building blocks of living things are available again and again.
Carbon, water and nitrogen are examples of materials that are cycled (AQA asks for the carbon cycle and the water cycle in detail).
The cycles link the **living world** (producers, consumers, decomposers) to the **non-living world** (atmosphere, oceans, soil, rocks).
Energy is different: it is **transferred** through ecosystems and is lost to the surroundings as heat, so it is not recycled. Matter is cycled, energy flows one way.
A **cycle** means a substance moves through several stores and returns to where it started, so the total amount stays the same even though it moves around.
These cycles explain why the **composition of the atmosphere** stays roughly constant in a stable ecosystem: removal and return of CO2 are balanced.
core.p: The Earth is essentially a closed system for matter: new atoms are not arriving in useful amounts, so the atoms that make up living things have to be **recycled** over and over again. Living organisms take elements such as carbon and the elements in water out of the environment to build their bodies, and they must eventually give them back so that other organisms can use them. If this did not happen, the raw materials of life would become locked up in dead bodies and living things would run out of them. The **carbon cycle** and the **water cycle** are two examples the specification asks you to know.

bullets: Carbon enters living things when **green plants and algae** take in carbon dioxide for **photosynthesis**.
Carbon passes along **food chains** when consumers eat producers and other consumers (feeding).
Carbon returns to the atmosphere as CO2 by **respiration** (plants, algae, animals and decomposers) and by **combustion** (burning wood and fossil fuels).
Dead organisms and waste are broken down by **decomposers**, which release carbon dioxide by respiration.
Over very long periods dead organisms can become **fossil fuels** (coal, oil, natural gas), which lock carbon away until they are burned.

Know the cycle as a **flow diagram**: atmosphere to producers (photosynthesis), producers to consumers (feeding), everything to atmosphere (respiration), dead matter to decomposers, fossil fuels to atmosphere (combustion).
core.h: The carbon cycle: the big picture
core.p: Carbon is found in all the **carbohydrates, lipids (fats) and proteins** that make up living things, so every living organism contains carbon. The main store of carbon that is available to living things is **carbon dioxide in the atmosphere**. The carbon cycle describes how carbon moves from the air into living things, between living things, and back into the air. In a stable community the processes that **remove** carbon dioxide from the air and the processes that **return** it are balanced, so the level of CO2 in the atmosphere stays roughly constant.

bullets: Word equation: carbon dioxide + water --(light energy)--> glucose + oxygen. Symbol equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O --> C6H12O6 + 6O2.
The glucose is used for respiration, or converted to **starch** (storage), **cellulose** (cell walls), **lipids** and, with nitrate ions from the soil, **proteins**.
Photosynthesis is an **endothermic** reaction: it transfers energy from the surroundings (light) to the chemicals.
Photosynthesis occurs only in the light, so in the day plants take in CO2 faster than they release it from respiration; the net effect is that they **remove** CO2.
Large areas of forest and the oceans' algae are important **carbon sinks** because they take in so much CO2.
Higher tier link: the rate of photosynthesis depends on light intensity, CO2 concentration and temperature, so changes in these change how fast carbon is removed.
core.p: Carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere by **green plants and algae** (including phytoplankton in the oceans) when they carry out **photosynthesis**. Light energy absorbed by chlorophyll is used to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. The carbon from the carbon dioxide is then used to make **carbohydrates, lipids and proteins** which make up the bodies of the plants and algae. This is the only way carbon from the air enters food chains, which is why producers are described as the 'entry point' of carbon into living things.

bullets: Use correct wording: carbon is passed on as **carbon compounds** (carbohydrates, proteins, fats) not as 'carbon dioxide'.
Carbon in the food that is **not digested** leaves the animal as faeces and is available to decomposers.
Only a small proportion of the carbon eaten is built into new biomass; much is released as CO2 in respiration, which links to **inefficient transfer of biomass** between trophic levels.
Example food chain: grass (producer) --> rabbit (primary consumer) --> fox (secondary consumer). Carbon compounds move along the arrows.
Arrows in a food chain show the direction of **energy and biomass transfer**, i.e. from the food to the organism that eats it.
Decomposers can be thought of as feeding on dead material and waste, so they also pass carbon compounds into their own bodies.
core.p: When an animal eats a plant (or eats another animal), the carbon compounds in the food, such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats, are passed into the consumer's body. Some of this carbon is built into the animal's own tissues, such as muscle (protein) and fat stores. The remainder is used in respiration or lost as waste. Feeding therefore moves carbon along the **food chain** from producers to primary consumers, then to secondary and tertiary consumers.

bullets: Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen --> carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released).
Respiration happens in **all living cells, day and night**; in plants it continues in the dark when photosynthesis has stopped.
In the light a plant usually photosynthesises faster than it respires, so overall it takes in CO2; at night it releases CO2.
Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) respire as they break down dead material, returning carbon as CO2, and are essential for completing the cycle.
Respiration is the main way carbon in **animal bodies** is returned to the air while the animals are alive.
Respiration is an **exothermic** reaction; the energy is used for movement, growth, active transport and keeping warm.
core.p: All living organisms respire all the time, **including plants and algae**. Respiration releases energy from glucose and produces carbon dioxide as a waste product, so carbon that was locked in organic compounds returns to the atmosphere. Plants, algae, animals and **decomposers** all respire, so every stage of the cycle returns some CO2. This is a very common exam point: students forget that plants respire as well as photosynthesise.

bullets: Decomposers are **microorganisms** (bacteria and fungi) which break down dead plant and animal matter and waste.
Their respiration returns the carbon to the atmosphere as **carbon dioxide**.
Decay also returns **mineral ions** (for example nitrates) to the soil, which plants take up through their roots.
Decay is faster in warm, moist conditions with plenty of oxygen (see the separate decomposition note).
If conditions are very cold, dry or lacking in oxygen, decay is slow, so carbon can stay locked away; this is how peat and, over millions of years, **fossil fuels** form.
Without decomposers, dead bodies and waste would pile up and nutrients would not be recycled.
core.p: When plants, algae and animals die, and when animals produce waste, the carbon compounds in them are broken down by **decomposers**, mainly bacteria and fungi. Decomposers secrete enzymes onto the dead material, digest it and absorb the soluble products. They use some of the products in their own **respiration**, which releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. In this way the carbon in dead bodies is not locked away permanently; it is cycled back so that producers can use it again.

bullets: Fossil fuels are **non-renewable** and formed from the remains of organisms over millions of years.
Burning fuel: hydrocarbon + oxygen --> carbon dioxide + water.
Combustion is a way of returning CO2 to the air that is **not part of respiration**; it is a big human-made addition to the cycle.
Forest fires (natural or deliberate) also release CO2 and reduce the number of trees that take CO2 in.
Many human activities such as power generation, transport and heating burn fossil fuels, raising atmospheric CO2.
Extra CO2 is a **greenhouse gas** that contributes to global warming (see the link to global warming below).
core.p: **Combustion** (burning) of wood and of **fossil fuels** (coal, oil and natural gas) releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Fossil fuels formed over millions of years from the remains of dead organisms that were buried and did not fully decay, so the carbon in them was locked away for a very long time. When we burn them, we release that stored carbon in a short period, which adds CO2 to the atmosphere faster than natural processes remove it. Burning wood releases carbon that was captured by trees more recently.

bullets: A **store** is where carbon is held (e.g. atmosphere, trees, fossil fuels); a **flow** is a process that moves carbon between stores (e.g. photosynthesis, respiration).
Fossil fuels are a very large but slowly changing store; burning moves carbon rapidly from this store to the atmosphere.
Forests and oceans take up large amounts of CO2 and are described as **carbon sinks**.
Do not invent exact quantities in exam answers; describe the direction and cause of changes.
If a question gives a diagram with arrows, read each arrow as a named process and say which process it represents.
Think: arrows into the atmosphere are respiration and combustion; arrows out of the atmosphere are photosynthesis.
core.h: Carbon in the oceans and other stores (extension)
core.p: Although the specification focuses on photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decay and combustion, you should understand that carbon is held in several **stores**: the atmosphere, living things, soil and dead matter, the oceans, and fossil fuels. Algae and phytoplankton in the sea photosynthesise and take in CO2 too, so the oceans are as important to the carbon cycle as land plants. Keeping the idea of 'stores' and 'flows' helps you to describe the cycle clearly and to answer data questions about what happens when a flow changes.

bullets: **Evaporation**: liquid water gains energy from the Sun and changes to water vapour (a gas) from oceans, rivers, lakes and soil.
**Transpiration** (from plants) adds water vapour from leaves, linked to the transpiration stream in the plant.
**Condensation**: water vapour cools as it rises and changes back into tiny droplets of liquid water, forming **clouds**.
**Precipitation**: water falls as rain, hail, sleet or snow when droplets in the clouds become large enough.
**Run-off and infiltration**: water flows over land into streams and rivers, or soaks into soil and rocks, and eventually returns to the sea.
The water cycle is driven by the **Sun's energy** and gravity (which makes water fall and flow downhill).
core.p: The **water cycle** provides **fresh water for plants and animals on land** before the water drains into the seas. It is powered by energy from the **Sun**. Water evaporates from the sea, lakes, rivers and the soil, and also from plants by transpiration. The water vapour rises, **condenses** as it cools to form clouds, and returns to the surface as **precipitation** (rain, hail, sleet or snow). Some runs over the land or soaks into the ground before returning to the sea, and the cycle begins again.

bullets: Plants take in water from the soil by **osmosis** through root hair cells; it is used in photosynthesis and to keep cells turgid.
Animals obtain water by drinking and in food; it is lost in sweat, urine and breath.
**Fresh water** is a limited resource; reservoirs and rivers rely on precipitation to refill.
Changes in the water cycle (for example drought) affect crop yields and ecosystems.
Water in the atmosphere (water vapour) is also a **greenhouse gas**.
The water cycle links to other topics: osmosis, transpiration, potable water production and weather.
core.h: Why the water cycle matters to living things
core.p: Living things need water for photosynthesis, to support cells, to transport substances, as a solvent in which reactions occur and to regulate temperature. Land organisms rely on **precipitation** to supply fresh water, because most of the Earth's water is salty sea water that most land plants and animals cannot use. The water cycle therefore constantly **renews** the supply of fresh water. Humans also depend on it to refill reservoirs, rivers and groundwater from which drinking water is obtained.

bullets: **Deforestation** reduces photosynthesis and, if the trees are burned or decay, releases stored carbon as CO2.
Deforestation of peat bogs (and burning of peat) releases large amounts of stored carbon.
Rising CO2 is linked to global warming, melting ice, sea level rise and changing weather patterns.
Possible solutions: planting trees (afforestation), reducing fossil fuel use, protecting forests and peat bogs, using renewable energy.
A common 6-mark question: link the human activity to a change in a **flow** of the carbon cycle, then to the effect on CO2 level, then to global warming.
Use cautious wording: 'contributes to', because climate change has several causes.
core.h: Linking the carbon cycle to human activity and global warming
core.p: Human activities can disturb the balance of the carbon cycle. **Burning fossil fuels** adds CO2 to the air, and **deforestation** removes trees that would have taken CO2 in by photosynthesis. Both processes make the level of atmospheric carbon dioxide rise. Carbon dioxide is a **greenhouse gas**: it absorbs infrared radiation emitted from the Earth's surface and re-emits some of it back, so it helps keep the Earth warm. More CO2 therefore increases the greenhouse effect and contributes to **global warming** and climate change.

bullets: Name arrows correctly: **photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, decay, combustion**. Avoid vague words like 'breathing' or 'absorbed'.
When a process stops or increases, state what happens to the **concentration of CO2** and why.
For percentage change calculations use (change / original) x 100.
Mention the **balance** of processes: in a stable ecosystem CO2 removed equals CO2 released.
In a 'what would happen if decomposers were removed' question: dead material builds up, less CO2 is returned, nutrients are not recycled to the soil.
State the cycle in the right order and use arrows or 'then' to show the sequence.
core.h: Exam skills: using cycle diagrams and data
core.p: Questions on cycles often give a diagram or data and ask you to name a process or explain a change. To name a process, work out what is happening: if carbon dioxide is going into a plant, it is photosynthesis; if carbon dioxide is coming out of anything living, it is respiration. If an arrow links a fuel to the air, it is combustion. For data questions, describe the trend with figures, then use your knowledge of the cycle to explain why.

exam: **Command words**: 'Name' (one word/phrase, 1 mark), 'Describe' (what happens, in order), 'Explain' (give a reason using 'because' or 'so that'), 'Evaluate' (weigh up both sides).
1-mark questions: name the process on an arrow (photosynthesis, respiration, combustion, feeding, decay). Use the exact word, not 'burning' for respiration.
2-mark questions: usually one fact and one link, e.g. 'Decomposers respire (1), releasing CO2 into the atmosphere (1)'.
3-4 mark 'describe the carbon cycle' answers should follow the carbon: CO2 in air --> photosynthesis --> carbon compounds in plants --> feeding --> animals --> respiration/decay --> CO2.
For 6-mark questions on human impact, use a clear chain: activity --> change in a process --> effect on CO2 level --> greenhouse effect --> global warming, then give a balanced conclusion.
Always state both **removal** (photosynthesis) and **return** (respiration, decay, combustion) when asked why CO2 level stays constant.
Model phrase: 'Plants take in carbon dioxide by photosynthesis and use the carbon to make glucose, which is used to make carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.'
Model phrase for the water cycle: 'Energy from the Sun causes water to evaporate; the water vapour cools and condenses to form clouds; water falls as precipitation.'
Graphs of CO2 level: describe the trend, quote start and end values with units (ppm), and calculate rate or percentage change when asked. Check axes and units first.
In diagrams, give the **process name** for arrows, and remember that arrows from living things to the air are respiration.
Do not mix up 'carbon' (the element) and 'carbon dioxide' (the compound that is in the air).
Check your answer addresses the context in the question (e.g. a forest, a pond, a farm) rather than giving a generic answer.

mistakes.r: All living things respire, including plants and algae. Plants also photosynthesise in the light.
mistakes.w: Plants only photosynthesise and animals only respire.

mistakes.r: Plants respire all the time (releasing CO2) and photosynthesise in the light (taking in CO2).
mistakes.w: Plants take in carbon and give out oxygen, so respiration is not needed.

mistakes.r: Decomposers respire as they break down dead material, releasing carbon dioxide back to the atmosphere.
mistakes.w: Decomposers are not part of the carbon cycle / 'decomposers make carbon'.

mistakes.r: Carbon is passed on as carbon compounds (carbohydrates, proteins, fats) in the food that is eaten.
mistakes.w: Carbon is passed along a food chain as carbon dioxide.

mistakes.r: Use scientific terms: trees absorb CO2 for photosynthesis and release O2 as a product; they also release CO2 by respiration.
mistakes.w: Trees 'breathe in' CO2 and 'breathe out' oxygen.

mistakes.r: Combustion is burning a fuel; respiration is a controlled chemical reaction in living cells. Both release CO2.
mistakes.w: Combustion is the same as respiration.

mistakes.r: Water evaporates, the vapour cools and condenses to form clouds, then falls as precipitation.
mistakes.w: Water evaporates and then 'turns into rain'.

mistakes.r: Water is not created or destroyed; it is recycled between stores and is renewed as fresh water by the cycle.
mistakes.w: The water cycle makes new water.

mistakes.r: Fossil fuels formed over millions of years from the remains of dead organisms (e.g. plankton and plants) buried and not fully decayed.
mistakes.w: Fossil fuels are made from dinosaurs.

summary: You must know how carbon is cycled between the atmosphere, living things, decomposers and fossil fuels through photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decay and combustion, and how the water cycle (evaporation, condensation, precipitation) supplies fresh water to living things on land. It matters because materials must be recycled for ecosystems to last, and because human activity can unbalance the carbon cycle.

terms.d: The cycling of carbon through the atmosphere, living organisms, soil and fossil fuels, by processes such as photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decay and combustion.
The process in which green plants and algae use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen, removing CO2 from the air.
The chemical reaction in all living cells that releases energy from glucose; aerobic respiration also produces carbon dioxide and water.
Burning of a fuel (wood or fossil fuel) in oxygen, releasing energy and carbon dioxide.
A fuel such as coal, oil or natural gas formed over millions of years from the remains of dead organisms.
A microorganism (bacterium or fungus) that breaks down dead plant and animal matter and waste.
The breakdown of dead organisms and waste by decomposers, returning carbon dioxide and mineral ions to the environment.
An organism, usually a green plant or alga, that makes its own food by photosynthesis and forms the start of a food chain.
An organism that gets its energy by eating other organisms.
The continuous movement of water between the sea, air and land by evaporation, condensation and precipitation, providing fresh water for living things.
The change of liquid water to water vapour, driven by heat energy from the Sun.
The change of water vapour to liquid water droplets as it cools, forming clouds.
Water falling from clouds to the ground as rain, hail, sleet or snow.
Loss of water vapour from the leaves of plants, mainly through the stomata.
A gas, such as carbon dioxide, methane or water vapour, that absorbs infrared radiation and helps to keep the Earth warm.
A store, such as forests or oceans, that takes in more carbon dioxide than it releases.

worked.ans: Plants absorb CO2 by photosynthesis and build the carbon into carbohydrates, lipids and proteins. The carbon compounds pass to the rabbit and then the fox by feeding. The fox returns carbon to the air as CO2 by respiration, and when it dies, decomposers break it down and release CO2 by respiration.
worked.q: Describe how carbon in the carbon dioxide in the air can become carbon in a fox, and then return to the air. (4 marks)
steps: Plants (producers) take in CO2 from the air and use it in photosynthesis (1).
The carbon is used to make carbohydrates, lipids and proteins in the plant (1).
A rabbit eats the plant and then the fox eats the rabbit, so carbon compounds are passed along the food chain by feeding (1).
The fox respires, releasing CO2 into the air; when it dies decomposers respire as they break down its body, also releasing CO2 (1).

worked.ans: Percentage increase = 50%. Combustion of fossil fuels and deforestation both increase atmospheric CO2, which is a greenhouse gas.
worked.q: The concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere was 280 ppm in 1750 and 420 ppm in 2023. Calculate the percentage increase, and explain two human activities that caused it. (5 marks)
steps: Burning fossil fuels in power stations, vehicles and heating releases CO2 by combustion that had been locked away for millions of years (1).
Deforestation removes trees, so less CO2 is removed by photosynthesis, and burning or decay of the trees releases CO2 (1).
The rise in CO2 increases the greenhouse effect, contributing to global warming (1).

worked.ans: Water evaporates due to the Sun's heat, condenses to form clouds, and falls as precipitation, giving land plants fresh water before it drains back to the sea.
worked.q: Explain how the water cycle provides fresh water for plants growing on land. (3 marks)
steps: Energy from the Sun causes water to evaporate from the sea, lakes and rivers (1).
The water vapour rises and cools, then condenses to form clouds (1).
Water falls as precipitation (rain, hail, sleet or snow) on to the land, where plants take it up through their roots before it drains into rivers and the sea (1).
